Construction of 2-solitons with logarithmic distance for the one-dimensional cubic Schrödinger system

Yvan Martel Address: CMLS, École Polytechnique, CNRS, 91128 Palaiseau, France Email address: yvan.martel@polytechnique.edu and Tiến Vinh Nguyễn Address: CMLS, École Polytechnique, CNRS, 91128 Palaiseau, France Email address: tien-vinh.nguyen@polytechnique.edu
Abstract.

We consider a system of coupled cubic Schrödinger equations in one space dimension

{i​∂tu+∂x2u+(|u|2+ω​|v|2)​u=0i​∂tv+∂x2v+(|v|2+ω​|u|2)​v=0(t,x)∈ℝ×ℝ,\begin{cases}\textnormal{i}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{2}u+(|u|^{2}+\omega|v|^{2})u=0\\ \textnormal{i}\partial_{t}v+\partial_{x}^{2}v+(|v|^{2}+\omega|u|^{2})v=0\end{cases}\quad(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R},

in the non-integrable case 0<ω<10<\omega<1.

First, we justify the existence of a symmetric 2-solitary wave with logarithmic distance, more precisely a solution of the system satisfying

limt→+∞‖(u⁡(t)v⁡(t))−(ei​tQ(⋅−12log(Ωt)−14loglogt)ei​tQ(⋅+12log(Ωt)+14loglogt))‖H1×H1=0\lim_{t\to+\infty}\left\|\begin{pmatrix}u(t)\\ v(t)\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}e^{\textnormal{i}t}Q(\cdot-\frac{1}{2}\log(\Omega t)-\frac{1}{4}\log\log t)\\[4.0pt] e^{\textnormal{i}t}Q(\cdot+\frac{1}{2}\log(\Omega t)+\frac{1}{4}\log\log t)\end{pmatrix}\right\|_{H^{1}\times H^{1}}=0

where Q=2​sechQ=\sqrt{2}\sech is the explicit solution of Q′′−Q+Q3=0Q^{\prime\prime}-Q+Q^{3}=0 and Ω>0\Omega>0 is a constant. This result extends to the non-integrable case the existence of symmetric 2-solitons with logarithmic distance known in the integrable case ω=0\omega=0 and ω=1\omega=1 ([15, 33]). Such strongly interacting symmetric 22-solitary waves were also previously constructed for the non-integrable scalar nonlinear Schrödinger equation in any space dimension and for any energy-subcritical power nonlinearity ([20, 22]).

Second, under the conditions 0<c<10<c<1 and 0<ω<12​c​(c+1)0<\omega<\frac{1}{2}c(c+1), we construct solutions of the system satisfying

limt→+∞‖(u⁡(t)v⁡(t))−(ei​c2​tQc(⋅−1(c+1)​clog(Ωct))ei​tQ(⋅+1c+1log(Ωct)))‖H1×H1=0\lim_{t\to+\infty}\left\|\begin{pmatrix}u(t)\\ v(t)\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}e^{\textnormal{i}c^{2}t}Q_{c}(\cdot-\frac{1}{(c+1)c}\log(\Omega_{c}t))\\[4.0pt] e^{\textnormal{i}t}Q(\cdot+\frac{1}{c+1}\log(\Omega_{c}t))\end{pmatrix}\right\|_{H^{1}\times H^{1}}=0

where Qc​(x)=c​Q​(c​x)Q_{c}(x)=cQ(cx) and Ωc>0\Omega_{c}>0 is a constant. Such logarithmic regime with non-symmetric solitons does not exist in the integrable cases ω=0\omega=0 and ω=1\omega=1 and is still unknown in the non-integrable scalar case.

1. Introduction

1.1. System of cubic Schrödinger equations

We consider the following one dimensional focusing-focusing system of coupled cubic Schrödinger equations

(coupled NLS) {i​∂tu+∂x2u+(|u|2+ω​|v|2)​u=0i​∂tv+∂x2v+(|v|2+ω​|u|2)​v=0(t,x)∈ℝ×ℝ\begin{cases}\textnormal{i}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{2}u+\left(|u|^{2}+\omega|v|^{2}\right)u=0\\ \textnormal{i}\partial_{t}v+\partial_{x}^{2}v+\left(|v|^{2}+\omega|u|^{2}\right)v=0\end{cases}\quad(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}

for u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x):ℝ×ℝ→ℂu(t,x),v(t,x):\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C} and for any parameter 0<ω<10<\omega<1. The initial data u​(0,x)=u0​(x)u(0,x)=u_{0}(x), v​(0,x)=v0​(x)v(0,x)=v_{0}(x) is taken in H1​(ℝ)×H1​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{1}(\mathbb{R}). The Hamiltonian system (coupled NLS) arises as a model for the propagation of the electrical field in nonlinear optics. Such systems also appear to model the interaction of two Bose-Einstein condensates in different spin states. See [1, 2, 32].

For ω=0\omega=0, the system (coupled NLS) simply reduces to two cubic focusing Schrödinger equations without coupling (see [1, 32, 33])

(cubic NLS) i​∂tu+∂x2u+|u|2​u=0(t,x)∈ℝ×ℝ.\textnormal{i}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{2}u+|u|^{2}u=0\quad(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}.

For ω=1\omega=1, the system (coupled NLS) is called the Manakov system (see [1, 15, 32])

(MS) {i​∂tu+∂x2u+(|u|2+|v|2)​u=0i​∂tv+∂x2v+(|v|2+|u|2)​v=0.\begin{cases}\textnormal{i}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{2}u+(|u|^{2}+|v|^{2})u=0\\ \textnormal{i}\partial_{t}v+\partial_{x}^{2}v+(|v|^{2}+|u|^{2})v=0.\end{cases}

Both (cubic NLS) and (MS) are completely integrable. For 0<ω<10<\omega<1, the system is not known to be integrable.

It follows from standard arguments (see e.g. [3, 10]) that the system (coupled NLS) is locally well-posed in H1×H1H^{1}\times H^{1}. In this paper, we work in the framework of such H1×H1H^{1}\times H^{1} solutions. Moreover, the system is invariant under the following symmetries:

  • •

    Phase: γ\gamma, γ′∈ℝ,(u0​(x)​ei​γv0​(x)​ei​γ′)↦(u⁡(t,x)​ei​γv⁡(t,x)​ei​γ′)\gamma^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R},\left(\begin{matrix}u_{0}(x)e^{\textnormal{i}\gamma}\\ v_{0}(x)e^{\textnormal{i}\gamma^{\prime}}\end{matrix}\right)\mapsto\left(\begin{matrix}u(t,x)e^{\textnormal{i}\gamma}\\ v(t,x)e^{\textnormal{i}\gamma^{\prime}}\end{matrix}\right);

  • •

    Scaling: λ>0\lambda>0, λ⁡(u0v0)​(λ​x)↦λ⁡(uv)​(λ2​t,λ​x)\lambda\left(\begin{matrix}u_{0}\\ v_{0}\end{matrix}\right)(\lambda x)\mapsto\lambda\left(\begin{matrix}u\\ v\end{matrix}\right)(\lambda^{2}t,\lambda x);

  • •

    Space translation: σ∈ℝ\sigma\in\mathbb{R}, (u0v0)​(x+σ)↦(uv)​(t,x+σ)\left(\begin{matrix}u_{0}\\ v_{0}\end{matrix}\right)(x+\sigma)\mapsto\left(\begin{matrix}u\\ v\end{matrix}\right)(t,x+\sigma);

  • •

    Galilean invariance: β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R}, ei​β​x​(u0v0)​(x)↦ei​β​(x−β​t)​(uv)​(t,x−2​β​t)e^{\textnormal{i}\beta x}\left(\begin{matrix}u_{0}\\ v_{0}\end{matrix}\right)(x)\mapsto e^{\textnormal{i}\beta(x-\beta t)}\left(\begin{matrix}u\\ v\end{matrix}\right)(t,x-2\beta t).

For H1×H1H^{1}\times H^{1} solutions, the following quantities are constant:

  • •

    Masses:

    M⁡(u⁡(t))=∫ℝ|u⁡(t,x)|2​𝑑x=M⁡(u0),M⁡(v⁡(t))=∫ℝ|v⁡(t,x)|2​𝑑x=M⁡(v0);M(u(t))=\int_{\mathbb{R}}|u(t,x)|^{2}dx=M(u_{0}),\quad M(v(t))=\int_{\mathbb{R}}|v(t,x)|^{2}dx=M(v_{0});
  • •

    Energy:

    E⁡(u⁡(t),v⁡(t))\displaystyle E(u(t),v(t)) =12​∫ℝ(|∂xu|2+|∂xv|2)​(t,x)​𝑑x−14​∫ℝ(|u|4+|v|4+2​ω​|u|2​|v|2)​(t,x)​𝑑x\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(|\partial_{x}u|^{2}+|\partial_{x}v|^{2}\right)(t,x)dx-\frac{1}{4}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(|u|^{4}+|v|^{4}+2\omega|u|^{2}|v|^{2}\right)(t,x)dx
    =E⁡(u0,v0);\displaystyle=E(u_{0},v_{0});
  • •

    Momentum:

    J(u(t),v(t))=ℑ∫ℝ∂xu(t,x)u¯(t,x)dx+ℑ∫ℝ∂xv(t,x)v¯(t,x)dx=J(u0,v0).J(u(t),v(t))=\Im\int_{\mathbb{R}}\partial_{x}u(t,x)\bar{u}(t,x)dx+\Im\int_{\mathbb{R}}\partial_{x}v(t,x)\bar{v}(t,x)dx=J(u_{0},v_{0}).

By the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality ‖u‖L44≲‖u‖L23​‖∂xu‖L2\|u\|_{L^{4}}^{4}\lesssim\|u\|_{L^{2}}^{3}\|\partial_{x}u\|_{L^{2}} and standard arguments, the system is globally well-posed in H1×H1H^{1}\times H^{1} (see e.g. [3, 28]).

Let QQ be the ground state, defined as

Q⁡(x)=2cosh⁡(x)​ unique (up to translation) H1 solution of Q′′−Q+Q3=0 on ℝ.Q(x)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\cosh(x)}\mbox{ unique (up to translation) $H^{1}$ solution of $Q^{\prime\prime}-Q+Q^{3}=0$ on $\mathbb{R}$.}

Recall that (cubic NLS) admits solitary wave solutions, also called solitons, of the form

u⁡(t,x)=ei​γ+i​λ2​t+i​β​(x−β​t)​Qλ​(x−σ−2​β​t)withQλ​(x)=λ​Q​(λ​x)u(t,x)=e^{\textnormal{i}\gamma+\textnormal{i}\lambda^{2}t+\textnormal{i}\beta(x-\beta t)}Q_{\lambda}(x-\sigma-2\beta t)\quad\text{with}\quad Q_{\lambda}(x)=\lambda Q(\lambda x)

where λ>0,γ,σ,β∈ℝ\lambda>0,\gamma,\sigma,\beta\in\mathbb{R}. When v=0v=0 (or u=0u=0), the system (coupled NLS) simplifies into (cubic NLS), and thus we deduce soliton solutions of (coupled NLS):

(uv)⁡(t,x)=(ei​Γ1​(t,x)​Qλ1​(x−σ1−2​β1​t)0),Γ1​(t,x)=γ1+λ12​t+β1​(x−β1​t)\begin{pmatrix}u\\ v\end{pmatrix}(t,x)=\begin{pmatrix}e^{\textnormal{i}\Gamma_{1}(t,x)}Q_{\lambda_{1}}(x-\sigma_{1}-2\beta_{1}t)\\ 0\end{pmatrix},\quad\Gamma_{1}(t,x)=\gamma_{1}+\lambda_{1}^{2}t+\beta_{1}(x-\beta_{1}t)

and

(uv)⁡(t,x)=(0ei​Γ2​(t,x)​Qλ2​(x−σ2−2​β2​t)),Γ2​(t,x)=γ2+λ22​t+β2​(x−β2​t)\begin{pmatrix}u\\ v\end{pmatrix}(t,x)=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ e^{\textnormal{i}\Gamma_{2}(t,x)}Q_{\lambda_{2}}(x-\sigma_{2}-2\beta_{2}t)\end{pmatrix},\quad\Gamma_{2}(t,x)=\gamma_{2}+\lambda_{2}^{2}t+\beta_{2}(x-\beta_{2}t)

for any λj>0,γj,σj,βj∈ℝ\lambda_{j}>0,\gamma_{j},\sigma_{j},\beta_{j}\in\mathbb{R} (j=1,2)(j=1,2). By definition, a multi-solitary wave (or multi-soliton) is a solution behaving in large time as a sum of such single solitons. In this article, we focus on 2-solitons such that one solitary wave is carried by uu and the other one by vv.

1.2. Previous results and motivation

Multi-solitons have been studied intensively in the integrable case, i.e. for (cubic NLS) and (MS), as well as for some nearly integrable models; see [1, 7, 8, 13, 24, 32, 33]. From the inverse scattering theory, there are three types of 2-solitons for (cubic NLS):

  • (a)

    Two solitons with different velocities: as t→+∞t\to+\infty, the distance between the solitons is of order tt ([33]).

  • (b)

    Double pole solutions: the two solitons have the same amplitude and their distance is logarithmic in tt ([24, 33]).

  • (c)

    Periodic 22-solitons: the two solitons have different amplitudes and their distance is a periodic function of time ([32, 33]).

More generally, the integrability theory treats the case of KK-solitary waves for any K≥2K\geq 2. Moreover, in the integrable case, multi-solitons have a pure soliton behavior for both t→+∞t\to+\infty and t→−∞t\to-\infty and describe the elastic interactions between solitons. For (MS), a trichotomy similar to (a)-(b)-(c) is studied formally and numerically in [31].

For non-integrable models, the study of multi-solitons is mostly limited to situations where solitons are decoupled, in particular, asymptotically in large time. Consider first the scalar nonlinear Schrödinger equation

(NLS) i​∂tu+Δ​u+|u|p−1​u=0,u⁡(0,x)=u0,(t,x)∈ℝ×ℝd,\textnormal{i}\partial_{t}u+\Delta u+|u|^{p-1}u=0,\quad u(0,x)=u_{0},\quad(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d},

in any space dimension d≥1d\geq 1 and for any energy subcritical power nonlinearity (i.e. p>1p>1 for d=1,2d=1,2 and 1<p<1+4d−21<p<1+\frac{4}{d-2} for d≥3d\geq 3). This equation is known to be completely integrable only for d=1d=1 and p=3p=3, i.e. (cubic NLS). Define the ground state QQ as the unique radial positive H1H^{1} solution (up to symmetries) of Δ​Q−Q+Qp=0\Delta Q-Q+Q^{p}=0 in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (for more properties of the ground state, see [3, 9, 25, 30]) and Qλ​(x)=λ2p−1​Q​(λ​x)Q_{\lambda}(x)=\lambda^{\frac{2}{p-1}}Q(\lambda x), for any λ>0\lambda>0. The existence of KK-solitary waves for (NLS) corresponding to case (a), i.e. solutions u⁡(t)u(t) of (NLS) such that

limt→+∞∥u(t)−∑k=1Ke−i​Γk​(t,⋅)Qλk(⋅−σk−2βkt)∥H1​(ℝd)=0\lim_{t\to+\infty}\bigg\|u(t)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}e^{-\textnormal{i}\Gamma_{k}(t,\cdot)}Q_{\lambda_{k}}(\cdot-\sigma_{k}-2\beta_{k}t)\bigg\|_{H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=0

for any λk>0\lambda_{k}>0 and any two-by-two different βk∈ℝd\beta_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, was established in [5, 17, 21].

Recently, the second author proved that the dynamics (b) is also a universal regime for (NLS), by constructing two symmetric solitary waves with logarithmic distance, [22]. The L2L^{2} critical case (p=1+4dp=1+\frac{4}{d}), previously studied in [20], exhibits a specific blow-up behavior also related to symmetric 22-solitons with logarithmic distance in rescaled variables.

Turning back to the system (coupled NLS) in the non-integrable case, i.e. for 0<ω<10<\omega<1, the existence of multi-solitary wave solutions corresponding to case (a)

limt→+∞‖(u⁡(t)v⁡(t))−(e−i​Γ1​(t,⋅)Qc(⋅−σ1−2β1t)e−i​Γ2​(t,⋅)Q(⋅−σ2−2β2t))‖H1=0,\lim_{t\to+\infty}\left\|\left(\begin{matrix}u(t)\\ v(t)\end{matrix}\right)-\left(\begin{matrix}e^{-\textnormal{i}\Gamma_{1}(t,\cdot)}Q_{c}(\cdot-\sigma_{1}-2\beta_{1}t)\\[2.0pt] e^{-\textnormal{i}\Gamma_{2}(t,\cdot)}Q(\cdot-\sigma_{2}-2\beta_{2}t)\end{matrix}\right)\right\|_{H^{1}}=0,

for any c>0c>0 and any different velocities β1≠β2\beta_{1}\neq\beta_{2} was proved in [6] (see also [11]).

A first goal of this paper is to justify the persistence of the regime (b) for the non-integrable (coupled NLS) in presence of symmetry, following the articles [20, 22] for the scalar (NLS) equation.

Second, and more importantly, we investigate the question of the (non-)persistence of the regime (c). Indeed, we exhibit a new logarithmic regime corresponding to non-symmetric 22-solitons with logarithmic distance which replaces the behavior (c). At the formal level, the system of parameters of the 22-solitons is not anymore integrable and periodic solutions disappear, see Remark 3. A logarithmic regime (see Theorem 2 and Remark 2) then takes place, which does not exist in the integrable cases ω=0\omega=0 and ω=1\omega=1. To our knowledge, such question is open for the scalar equation (NLS) in the non-integrable case (see Section 5).

1.3. Main results.

First, we present the symmetric logarithmic regime.

Theorem 1.

For any 0<ω<10<\omega<1, there exists a solution (uv)∈𝒞⁡(ℝ,H1×H1)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}u\\ v\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbb{R},H^{1}\times H^{1}) of (coupled NLS) such that

limt→+∞‖(u⁡(t)v⁡(t))−(ei​tQ(⋅−12log(Ωt)−14loglogt)ei​tQ(⋅+12log(Ωt)+14loglogt))‖H1×H1=0\lim_{t\to+\infty}\left\|\left(\begin{matrix}u(t)\\ v(t)\end{matrix}\right)-\left(\begin{matrix}e^{\textnormal{i}t}Q(\cdot-\frac{1}{2}\log(\Omega t)-\frac{1}{4}\log\log t)\\[4.0pt] e^{\textnormal{i}t}Q(\cdot+\frac{1}{2}\log(\Omega t)+\frac{1}{4}\log\log t)\end{matrix}\right)\right\|_{H^{1}\times H^{1}}=0

where Ω>0\Omega>0 is a constant depending on ω\omega.

Note that as t→+∞t\to+\infty, the distance between the two solitary waves is asymptotic to

(1.1) y⁡(t)=log⁡t+12​log⁡log⁡t+log⁡Ω.y(t)=\log t+\frac{1}{2}\log\log t+\log\Omega.
Remark 1.

An analogous dynamics was constructed for (cubic NLS) in [24, 33] and for (NLS) in [20, 22].

Second, we construct for (coupled NLS) a new logarithmic dynamics of 2-solitary waves with different amplitude.

Theorem 2.

For any 0<c<10<c<1 and 0<ω<12​c​(c+1)<10<\omega<\frac{1}{2}c(c+1)<1, there exists a solution (uv)∈𝒞⁡(ℝ,H1×H1)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}u\\ v\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbb{R},H^{1}\times H^{1}) of (coupled NLS) such that

limt→+∞‖(u⁡(t)v⁡(t))−(ei​c2​tQc(⋅−1(c+1)​clog(Ωct))ei​tQ(⋅+1c+1log(Ωct)))‖H1×H1=0\lim_{t\to+\infty}\left\|\left(\begin{matrix}u(t)\\ v(t)\end{matrix}\right)-\left(\begin{matrix}e^{\textnormal{i}c^{2}t}Q_{c}(\cdot-\frac{1}{(c+1)c}\log(\Omega_{c}t))\\[4.0pt] e^{\textnormal{i}t}Q(\cdot+\frac{1}{c+1}\log(\Omega_{c}t))\end{matrix}\right)\right\|_{H^{1}\times H^{1}}=0

where Ωc>0\Omega_{c}>0 is a constant depending on cc and ω\omega.

Note that as t→+∞t\to+\infty, the distance between the two solitary waves is asymptotic to

(1.2) yc​(t)=1c​log⁡t+1c​log⁡Ωc.y_{c}(t)=\frac{1}{c}\log t+\frac{1}{c}\log\Omega_{c}\,.

As mentioned before, such solution does not exist in the integrable cases and the analogous question for the non-integrable scalar equation (NLS) seems open. See Section 5.

Remark 2.

The slight difference between the two regimes (1.1) and (1.2) is due to stronger interactions when solitary waves have equal amplitudes. We refer to Sections 4.2 and 2.3 for formal derivations of the regimes (1.1) and (1.2).

We believe that there is no other logarithmic regime for (coupled NLS). In support of this conjecture, we refer to the case of the generalized Korteweg-de Vries equation, for which existence of a logarithmic regime was proved in [23] and uniqueness (in the super-critical case) was established in [12].

The case 12​c​(c+1)≤ω<1\frac{1}{2}c(c+1)\leq\omega<1 in Theorem 2 is open (see step 1 of the proof of Proposition 1).

Remark 3.

The dynamics of the distance between the two solitary waves is related to nonlinear interactions. A formal study (see notably [8, 13] and Chapter 4 in [32]) shows that the three behaviors (a), (b) and (c) are related to different solutions of

{γ¨=cγ​e−σ​sin⁡γσ¨=−cσ​e−σ​cos⁡γ\begin{cases}\ddot{\gamma}=c_{\gamma}e^{-\sigma}\sin\gamma\\ \ddot{\sigma}=-c_{\sigma}e^{-\sigma}\cos\gamma\end{cases}

where γ\gamma is the phase difference, σ\sigma the relative distance and cγc_{\gamma}, cσc_{\sigma} are constants. For (cubic NLS), it holds cγ=cσ>0c_{\gamma}=c_{\sigma}>0. Denoting Y=σ+i​γY=\sigma+\textnormal{i}\gamma, the resulting equation Y¨=−cγ​eY\ddot{Y}=-c_{\gamma}e^{Y} is integrable and admits nontrivial solutions for which σ\sigma is periodic.

Remark 4.

The proofs of Theorems 1 and 2 follow the overall strategy of several previous articles on multi-solitons ([14, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 26]), particularly of [20, 22] which started the study of multi-solitons with logarithmic distance in a non-integrable setting. We focus on the proof of Theorem 2, which is more original in the construction of a suitable approximate solution and the determination of the asymptotic regime (see Remark 5).

See Section 5 for a comment on the introduction of a refined energy method.

1.4. Notation and preliminaries

fλ(x)=λf(λx)andΛf(x)=f(x)+xf′(x)=∂λfλ(x)|λ=1.f_{\lambda}(x)=\lambda f(\lambda x)\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Lambda f(x)=f(x)+xf^{\prime}(x)=\partial_{\lambda}f_{\lambda}(x)_{|\lambda=1}.

(1.4) 0<c≤1and0<ω<c⁡(c+1)2.0<c\leq 1\quad\mbox{and}\quad 0<\omega<\frac{c(c+1)}{2}.

The linearization of  (coupled NLS) around solitons involves the following operators:

ℒ+=−∂x2+1−3Q2,ℒ−=−∂x2+1−Q2,ℒc=−∂x2+c2−ωQ2.\mathcal{L}_{+}=-\partial_{x}^{2}+1-3Q^{2},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{-}=-\partial_{x}^{2}+1-Q^{2},\quad\mathcal{L}_{c}=-\partial_{x}^{2}+c^{2}-\omega Q^{2}.

Recall the special relations ([29])

(1.5) ℒ−​Q=0,ℒ+​(Λ​Q)=−2​Q,ℒ+​(Q′)=0,ℒ−​(x​Q)=−2​Q′.\mathcal{L}_{-}Q=0,\quad\mathcal{L}_{+}(\Lambda Q)=-2Q,\quad\mathcal{L}_{+}(Q^{\prime})=0,\quad\mathcal{L}_{-}(xQ)=-2Q^{\prime}.

We will use the following properties of these operators.

Lemma 1.

Assume (1.4).

  1. (i)

    There exists μ>0\mu>0 such that, for all z∈H1z\in H^{1},

    ⟨ℒ+​ℜ⁡z,ℜ⁡z⟩+⟨ℒ−​ℑ⁡z,ℑ⁡z⟩≥μ​‖z‖H12−1μ​(⟨z,Q⟩2+⟨z,x​Q⟩2+⟨z,i​Λ​Q⟩2),\displaystyle\langle\mathcal{L}_{+}\Re z,\Re z\rangle+\langle\mathcal{L}_{-}\Im z,\Im z\rangle\geq\mu\|z\|_{H^{1}}^{2}-\frac{1}{\mu}\left(\langle z,Q\rangle^{2}+\langle z,xQ\rangle^{2}+\langle z,\textnormal{i}\Lambda Q\rangle^{2}\right),
    ⟨ℒc​z,z⟩≥μ​‖z‖H12.\displaystyle\langle\mathcal{L}_{c}z,z\rangle\geq\mu\|z\|^{2}_{H^{1}}.
  2. (ii)

    For any f∈L2f\in L^{2}, there exists a unique solution u∈H2u\in H^{2} of ℒc​u=f\mathcal{L}_{c}u=f. Moreover,

    • –

      If |f⁡(x)|≲e−λ​|x||f(x)|\lesssim e^{-\lambda|x|} for some λ>c\lambda>c, then |u⁡(x)|≲e−c​|x||u(x)|\lesssim e^{-c|x|}.

(i) The coercivity properties of ℒ+\mathcal{L}_{+} and ℒ−\mathcal{L}_{-} (here in the L2L^{2} sub-critical case) are well-known facts (see e.g. [17, 29, 30]).

Let 0<ρ<c0<\rho<c be such that ω=12​ρ​(ρ+1)\omega=\frac{1}{2}\rho(\rho+1). By [27] or direct computation, we see that the positive function QρQ^{\rho} satisfies ℒc​Qρ=(c2−ρ2)​Qρ\mathcal{L}_{c}Q^{\rho}=(c^{2}-\rho^{2})Q^{\rho}. The coercivity property follows.

(ii) Let c≤λ≤1c\leq\lambda\leq 1. If ℒc​u=f\mathcal{L}_{c}u=f with |f⁡(x)|≲e−λ​|x||f(x)|\lesssim e^{-\lambda|x|} then −u′′+c2​u=g-u^{\prime\prime}+c^{2}u=g where g=f+ω​Q2​ug=f+\omega Q^{2}u also satisfies |g⁡(x)|≲e−λ​|x||g(x)|\lesssim e^{-\lambda|x|}. The decay properties of uu then follows from standard arguments. ∎

The following result follows directly from Lemma 1.

Lemma 2.
  1. (i)

    (1.6) ℒc​A=−A′′+c2​A−ω​Q2​A=c​κ​ω​ec​x​Q2\mathcal{L}_{c}A=-A^{\prime\prime}+c^{2}A-\omega Q^{2}A=c\kappa\omega e^{cx}Q^{2}

2. Approximate solution in the case 0<c<10<c<1

2.1. Definition of the approximate solution

Consider 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} time-dependent real-valued functions σ1\sigma_{1}, σ2\sigma_{2}, γ1\gamma_{1}, γ2\gamma_{2}, β1\beta_{1}, β2\beta_{2}, to be fixed later and set

σ=σ1−σ2,β=β1−β2,γ=γ1−γ2.\sigma=\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{2},\quad\beta=\beta_{1}-\beta_{2},\quad\gamma=\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2}.

∂1P=Qc′​(x−σ1)​ei​Γ1,x1​P=(x−σ1)​P,Λ1​P=Λ​Qc​(x−σ1)​ei​Γ1,\displaystyle\partial_{1}P=Q_{c}^{\prime}(x-\sigma_{1})e^{\textnormal{i}\Gamma_{1}},\quad x_{1}P=(x-\sigma_{1})P,\quad\Lambda_{1}P=\Lambda Q_{c}(x-\sigma_{1})e^{\textnormal{i}\Gamma_{1}},

∂2R=Q′​(x−σ2)​ei​Γ2,x2​R=(x−σ2)​R,Λ2​R=Λ​Q​(x−σ2)​ei​Γ2.\displaystyle\partial_{2}R=Q^{\prime}(x-\sigma_{2})e^{\textnormal{i}\Gamma_{2}},\quad x_{2}R=(x-\sigma_{2})R,\quad\Lambda_{2}R=\Lambda Q(x-\sigma_{2})e^{\textnormal{i}\Gamma_{2}}.

𝐙=(UV)and setℰ𝐙=(ℰUℰV)=(i​∂tU+∂x2U+(|U|2+ω​|V|2)​Ui​∂tV+∂x2V+(|V|2+ω​|U|2)​V).\mathbf{Z}=\begin{pmatrix}U\\ V\end{pmatrix}\quad\mbox{and set}\quad\mathcal{E}_{\mathbf{Z}}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{E}_{U}\\ \mathcal{E}_{V}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\textnormal{i}\partial_{t}U+\partial_{x}^{2}U+\left(|U|^{2}+\omega|V|^{2}\right)U\\[4.0pt] \textnormal{i}\partial_{t}V+\partial_{x}^{2}V+\left(|V|^{2}+\omega|U|^{2}\right)V\end{pmatrix}.

It holds

(2.1) {ℰU=F−m→1⋅M→1−m→φ⋅M→φℰV=G−m→2⋅M→2\left\{\begin{aligned} \mathcal{E}_{U}&=F-\vec{m}_{1}\cdot\vec{\textnormal{M}}_{1}-\vec{m}_{\varphi}\cdot\vec{\textnormal{M}}_{\varphi}\\ \mathcal{E}_{V}&=G-\vec{m}_{2}\cdot\vec{\textnormal{M}}_{2}\end{aligned}\right.

where

a=12​c​⟨F,∂1P⟩andb=12​⟨G,∂2R⟩.a=\frac{1}{2c}{\langle F,\partial_{1}P\rangle}\quad\mbox{and}\quad b=\frac{1}{2}{\langle G,\partial_{2}R\rangle}.

2.3. Formal discussion

Formally, the previous computations lead us to the system

σ˙1=2​β1,β˙1=−αc​e−2​c​σ,σ˙2=2​β2,β˙2=c​αc​e−2​c​σ.\dot{\sigma}_{1}=2\beta_{1},\quad\dot{\beta}_{1}=-\alpha_{c}e^{-2c\sigma},\quad\dot{\sigma}_{2}=2\beta_{2},\quad\dot{\beta}_{2}=c\alpha_{c}e^{-2c\sigma}.

Recalling σ=σ1−σ2\sigma=\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{2} and β=β1−β2\beta=\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}, this gives

σ¨=−2​(c+1)​αc​e−2​c​σ,2​β=σ˙,\ddot{\sigma}=-2(c+1)\alpha_{c}e^{-2c\sigma},\quad 2\beta={\dot{\sigma}},

which admits the following solution

σ(t)=1clog(Ωct),2β(t)=1c​t=Ωcce−c​σwhereΩc=[2c(c+1)αc]12>0.\sigma(t)=\frac{1}{c}\log(\Omega_{c}t),\quad 2\beta(t)=\frac{1}{ct}=\frac{\Omega_{c}}{c}e^{-c\sigma}\quad\mbox{where}\quad\Omega_{c}=[2c(c+1)\alpha_{c}]^{\frac{1}{2}}>0.

This justifies the existence of the regime (1.2) of Theorem 2. In particular, observe that the positive sign of the constant αc\alpha_{c} is responsible for the emergence of the special non-symmetric logarithmic regime. The phase parameters γ1\gamma_{1} and γ2\gamma_{2} are not essential for the dynamics and so we do not discuss them here.

Let T∞≫1T_{\infty}\gg 1 to be fixed later and consider a solution (uv)\big(\begin{smallmatrix}u\\ v\end{smallmatrix}\big) of (coupled NLS) under the form

Then, using the notation

h⁡(u,v)=(|u|2+ω​|v|2)​uh(u,v)=\left(|u|^{2}+\omega|v|^{2}\right)u

the function (εη)\big(\begin{smallmatrix}\varepsilon\\ \eta\end{smallmatrix}\big) satisfies the system

(2.9) {i​∂tε+∂x2ε+h⁡(U+ε,V+η)−h⁡(U,V)+ℰU=0i​∂tη+∂x2η+h⁡(V+η,U+ε)−h⁡(V,U)+ℰV=0\left\{\begin{aligned} &\textnormal{i}\partial_{t}\varepsilon+\partial_{x}^{2}\varepsilon+h(U+\varepsilon,V+\eta)-h(U,V)+\mathcal{E}_{U}=0\\ &\textnormal{i}\partial_{t}\eta+\partial_{x}^{2}\eta+h(V+\eta,U+\varepsilon)-h(V,U)+\mathcal{E}_{V}=0\end{aligned}\right.

The parameters σ1\sigma_{1}, σ2\sigma_{2}, γ1\gamma_{1}, γ2\gamma_{2}, β1\beta_{1} and β2\beta_{2} in the definition of (UV)\big(\begin{smallmatrix}U\\ V\end{smallmatrix}\big) are fixed by imposing the following orthogonality conditions

(2.10) {⟨ε,x1​P⟩=⟨ε,i​Λ1​P⟩=⟨ε,i​∂1P⟩=0⟨η,x2​R⟩=⟨η,i​Λ2​R⟩=⟨η,i​∂2R⟩=0\left\{\begin{aligned} &\langle\varepsilon,x_{1}P\rangle=\langle\varepsilon,\textnormal{i}\Lambda_{1}P\rangle=\langle\varepsilon,\textnormal{i}\partial_{1}P\rangle=0\\ &\langle\eta,x_{2}R\rangle=\langle\eta,\textnormal{i}\Lambda_{2}R\rangle=\langle\eta,\textnormal{i}\partial_{2}R\rangle=0\end{aligned}\right.

and initial conditions

(2.11) {σ1(T∞)=σ∞c+1,σ2(T∞)=−c​σ∞c+1,β1(T∞)=β∞c+1,β2(T∞)=−c​β∞c+1,γ1(T∞)=0,γ2(T∞)=0,\left\{\begin{aligned} &\sigma_{1}(T_{\infty})=\frac{\sigma_{\infty}}{c+1},\quad\sigma_{2}(T_{\infty})=-\frac{c\sigma_{\infty}}{c+1},\\ &\beta_{1}(T_{\infty})=\frac{\beta_{\infty}}{c+1},\quad\beta_{2}(T_{\infty})=-\frac{c\beta_{\infty}}{c+1},\\ &\gamma_{1}(T_{\infty})=0,\quad\gamma_{2}(T_{\infty})=0,\end{aligned}\right.

where σ∞\sigma_{\infty} is to be chosen later close to 1c​log⁡(Ωc​T∞)\frac{1}{c}\log(\Omega_{c}T_{\infty}) (see below (3.2)) and

(2.12) β∞=Ωc2​c​e−c​σ∞.\beta_{\infty}=\frac{\Omega_{c}}{2c}e^{-c\sigma_{\infty}}.

Indeed, by a standard argument and the initial conditions (including ε⁡(T∞)=η⁡(T∞)=0\varepsilon(T_{\infty})=\eta(T_{\infty})=0), the orthogonality conditions are equivalent to a first order differential system in the parameters (σ1,σ2,γ1,γ2,β1,β2)(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\beta_{1},\beta_{2}), which admits a unique local solution in the regime considered in this paper. See e.g. Lemma 2.7 in  [4] for a detailled argument in the case of the (gKdV) equation, and Lemma 7 in the present paper for the corresponding estimates on the time derivatives of the parameters. For technical reasons, one can fix zero initial conditions on γ1\gamma_{1}, γ2\gamma_{2} as in (2.11), but the initial conditions on σ1\sigma_{1}, σ2\sigma_{2}, β1\beta_{1} and β2\beta_{2} have to depend on a parameter σ∞\sigma_{\infty} to be fixed later by a topological argument.

As in [20, 22, 26], the orthogonality conditions in (2.10) are related to (1.5). Using the conservation of masses and L2L^{2} sub-criticality, we avoid the modulation of the scaling parameters of the solitons (see [30] and the proof of Lemma 7).

3.3. Energy estimates

Let

H⁡(u,v)=14​|u|4+14​|v|4+ω2​|u|2​|v|2,h⁡(u,v)=(|u|2+ω​|v|2)​u.H(u,v)=\dfrac{1}{4}|u|^{4}+\dfrac{1}{4}|v|^{4}+\dfrac{\omega}{2}|u|^{2}|v|^{2},\quad h(u,v)=(|u|^{2}+\omega|v|^{2})u.

d2​H​(U,V)​(η)=12​(|V|2+ω​|U|2)​(V​η¯+V¯​η)=ℜ⁡(h⁡(V,U)​η),\displaystyle d_{2}H(U,V)(\eta)=\dfrac{1}{2}(|V|^{2}+\omega|U|^{2})(V\bar{\eta}+\bar{V}\eta)=\Re\left(h(V,U)\eta\right),
d1​h​(U,V)​(ε)=2​|U|2​ε+U2​ε¯+ω​|V|2​ε,d2​h​(U,V)​(η)=ω⁡(V​η¯+V¯​η)​U,\displaystyle d_{1}h(U,V)(\varepsilon)=2|U|^{2}\varepsilon+U^{2}\bar{\varepsilon}+\omega|V|^{2}\varepsilon,\quad d_{2}h(U,V)(\eta)=\omega(V\bar{\eta}+\bar{V}\eta)U,

𝐊(t,ε,η)=12∫{|∂xε|2+|∂xη|2−2[H(U+ε,V+η)−H(U,V)−d1H(U,V)(ε)−d2H(U,V)(η)]}\mathbf{K}(t,\varepsilon,\eta)=\dfrac{1}{2}\int\big\{|\partial_{x}\varepsilon|^{2}+|\partial_{x}\eta|^{2}-2\big[H(U+\varepsilon,V+\eta)-H(U,V)\\ -d_{1}H(U,V)(\varepsilon)-d_{2}H(U,V)(\eta)\big]\big\}

𝐌=M1+M2,M1​(ε)=c22​∫|ε|2,M2​(η)=12​∫|η|2.\mathbf{M}=M_{1}+M_{2},\quad M_{1}(\varepsilon)=\dfrac{c^{2}}{2}\int|\varepsilon|^{2},\quad M_{2}(\eta)=\dfrac{1}{2}\int|\eta|^{2}.

Let χ:[0,+∞)→[0,+∞)\chi:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty) be a smooth non-increasing function satisfying χ≡1\chi\equiv 1 on [0,14][0,\frac{1}{4}] and χ≡0\chi\equiv 0 on [12,+∞)[\frac{1}{2},+\infty). Denote 𝐉=J1+J2\mathbf{J}=J_{1}+J_{2} where, for j=1,2j=1,2,

Jj​(t,ε,η)=βj​ℑ​∫[(∂xε)​ε¯+(∂xη)​η¯]​χjwhereχj​(t,x)=χ⁡(|x−σj​(t)|log⁡t).J_{j}(t,\varepsilon,\eta)=\beta_{j}\,\Im\int\left[(\partial_{x}\varepsilon)\bar{\varepsilon}+(\partial_{x}\eta)\bar{\eta}\right]\chi_{j}\quad\mbox{where}\quad\chi_{j}(t,x)=\chi\left(\frac{|x-\sigma_{j}(t)|}{\log t}\right).

𝐒⁡(t,ε,η)=⟨ε,F⟂⟩+2​β​⟨ε,i​ϕ⟩+⟨η,G⟂⟩whereϕ=∂1φ−c​φ.\mathbf{S}(t,\varepsilon,\eta)=\langle\varepsilon,F^{\perp}\rangle+2\beta\langle\varepsilon,\textnormal{i}\phi\rangle+\langle\eta,G^{\perp}\rangle\quad\mbox{where}\quad\phi=\partial_{1}\varphi-c\varphi.

Under the bootstrap (3.1), we prove the following estimates.

Proposition 1.

Let θ1<θ<min⁡{1c;2}\theta_{1}<\theta<\min\{\frac{1}{c};2\}. It holds

(3.13) ‖ε‖H12+‖η‖H12≲𝐖⁡(t,ε,η)+C​t−2​θ,\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\eta\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\lesssim\mathbf{W}(t,\varepsilon,\eta)+Ct^{-2\theta},

Proof of Proposition 1.

step 1. The coercivity property (3.13) is a consequence of the coercivity property around one solitary wave in Lemma 1, the orthogonality relations (2.10)-(3.8)) and the positivity of ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c}. It also involves a localization argument similar to the proof of Lemma 4.1 in [19] for the scalar case.

Note that by (3.1),

|𝐉⁡(t,ε,η)|≲t−1​(‖ε‖H12+‖η‖H12)|\mathbf{J}(t,\varepsilon,\eta)|\lesssim t^{-1}(\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\eta\|_{H^{1}}^{2})

and by (3.4) and (3.6),

∫(|P​φ|+|φ|2)​|ε|2+∫|U​ε|​|V​η|≲t−1​(‖ε‖H12+‖η‖H12).\int(|P\varphi|+|\varphi|^{2})|\varepsilon|^{2}+\int|U\varepsilon||V\eta|\lesssim t^{-1}\left(\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\eta\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\right).

Moreover, cubic and higher order terms in ε\varepsilon or η\eta are of order t−θ1​(‖ε‖H12+‖η‖H12)t^{-\theta_{1}}\left(\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\eta\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\right).

Therefore, we are reduced to consider the following two decoupled functionals

𝐖1\displaystyle\mathbf{W}_{1} =∫{|∂xε|2+c2​|ε|2−|P|2​|ε|2−2​[ℜ⁡(P​ε¯)]2−ω​|R|2​|ε|2},\displaystyle=\int\left\{|\partial_{x}\varepsilon|^{2}+c^{2}|\varepsilon|^{2}-|P|^{2}|\varepsilon|^{2}-2[\Re(P\bar{\varepsilon})]^{2}-\omega|R|^{2}|\varepsilon|^{2}\right\},
𝐖2\displaystyle\mathbf{W}_{2} =∫{|∂xη|2+|η|2−|R|2​|η|2−2​[ℜ⁡(R​η¯)]2−ω​|P|2​|η|2}.\displaystyle=\int\left\{|\partial_{x}\eta|^{2}+|\eta|^{2}-|R|^{2}|\eta|^{2}-2[\Re(R\bar{\eta})]^{2}-\omega|P|^{2}|\eta|^{2}\right\}.

We focus on the coercivity property for 𝐖1\mathbf{W}_{1}, the case of 𝐖2\mathbf{W}_{2} is similar.

Denote Φ:ℝ→ℝ\Phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} an even function of class 𝒞2\mathcal{C}^{2} such that

Let B>1B>1 and ΦB​(x)=Φ⁡(x/B)\Phi_{B}(x)=\Phi(x/B). We claim that for BB large enough, there exists μ1>0\mu_{1}>0, such that for any ε^\hat{\varepsilon} satisfying ⟨ε^,Q⟩=⟨ε^,x​Q⟩=⟨ε^,i​Λ​Q⟩=0\langle\hat{\varepsilon},Q\rangle=\langle\hat{\varepsilon},xQ\rangle=\langle\hat{\varepsilon},\textnormal{i}\Lambda Q\rangle=0, and any ε~\tilde{\varepsilon}, it holds

𝒩1​(ε^)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{1}(\hat{\varepsilon}) :=∫ΦB​{|∂xε^|2+|ε^|2−Q2​|ε^|2−2​[ℜ⁡(Q​ε^¯)]2}≥μ1​∫ΦB​(|∂xε^|2+|ε^|2),\displaystyle:=\int\Phi_{B}\left\{|\partial_{x}\hat{\varepsilon}|^{2}+|\hat{\varepsilon}|^{2}-Q^{2}|\hat{\varepsilon}|^{2}-2\left[\Re(Q\bar{\hat{\varepsilon}})\right]^{2}\right\}\geq\mu_{1}\int\Phi_{B}(|\partial_{x}\hat{\varepsilon}|^{2}+|\hat{\varepsilon}|^{2}),
𝒩2​(ε~)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{2}(\tilde{\varepsilon}) :=∫ΦB​{|∂xε~|2+c2​|ε~|2−ω​Q2​|ε~|2}≥μ1​∫ΦB​(|∂xε~|2+|ε~|2).\displaystyle:=\int\Phi_{B}\left\{|\partial_{x}\tilde{\varepsilon}|^{2}+c^{2}|\tilde{\varepsilon}|^{2}-{\omega}Q^{2}|\tilde{\varepsilon}|^{2}\right\}\geq\mu_{1}\int\Phi_{B}(|\partial_{x}\tilde{\varepsilon}|^{2}+|\tilde{\varepsilon}|^{2}).

Setting z=ε^​ΦB12z=\hat{\varepsilon}\Phi_{B}^{\frac{1}{2}} and following the proof of Claim 8 in [19], the coercivity of 𝒩1\mathcal{N}_{1} follows from (i) of Lemma 1 applied to the function zz. A similar localization argument, using the coercivity property of ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c} proves the estimate for 𝒩2​(ε~)\mathcal{N}_{2}(\tilde{\varepsilon}) without any orthogonality condition on ε~\tilde{\varepsilon}. This is where our proof needs the condition (1.4).

Using these estimates with ε^\hat{\varepsilon} and ε~\tilde{\varepsilon} such that ε=c​ε^​(c⁡(x−σ1))​ei​Γ1\varepsilon=c\hat{\varepsilon}(c(x-\sigma_{1}))e^{\textnormal{i}\Gamma_{1}} and ε=ε~​(x−σ2)​ei​Γ2\varepsilon=\tilde{\varepsilon}(x-\sigma_{2})e^{\textnormal{i}\Gamma_{2}}, the orthogonality conditions (2.10) and the almost orthogonality relation (3.8), we obtain the estimate ‖ε‖H12≲𝐖1+t−4​(log⁡t)2\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\lesssim\mathbf{W}_{1}+t^{-4}(\log t)^{2}.

step 2. Time variation of the energy. Denote

+β1​⟨i​∂tε,2​χ1​∂xε+ε​∂xχ1⟩+β1​⟨i​∂tη,2​χ1​∂xη+η​∂xχ1⟩.\displaystyle\quad+\beta_{1}\langle\textnormal{i}\partial_{t}\varepsilon,2\chi_{1}\partial_{x}\varepsilon+\varepsilon\partial_{x}\chi_{1}\rangle+\beta_{1}\langle\textnormal{i}\partial_{t}\eta,2\chi_{1}\partial_{x}\eta+\eta\partial_{x}\chi_{1}\rangle.

and so by (3.1), (3.9) and the properties of χ\chi, |∂tχj|≲t−1​(log⁡t)−1|\partial_{t}\chi_{j}|\lesssim t^{-1}(\log t)^{-1}. It follows that

|β1​ℑ​∫[(∂xε)​ε¯+(∂xη)​η¯]​∂tχ1|≲t−2​(log⁡t)−1​(‖ε‖H12+‖η‖H22)≲t−2−2​θ1​(log⁡t)−1.\left|\beta_{1}\Im\int[(\partial_{x}\varepsilon)\overline{\varepsilon}+(\partial_{x}\eta)\overline{\eta}]\partial_{t}\chi_{1}\right|\lesssim t^{-2}(\log t)^{-1}\left(\|\varepsilon\|^{2}_{H^{1}}+\|\eta\|_{H^{2}}^{2}\right)\lesssim t^{-2-2\theta_{1}}(\log t)^{-1}.

⟨i​∂tε,2​χ1​∂xε+ε​∂xχ1⟩\displaystyle\langle\textnormal{i}\partial_{t}\varepsilon,2\chi_{1}\partial_{x}\varepsilon+\varepsilon\partial_{x}\chi_{1}\rangle =−⟨∂x2ε,2​χ1​∂xε+ε​∂xχ1⟩\displaystyle=-\langle\partial_{x}^{2}\varepsilon,2\chi_{1}\partial_{x}\varepsilon+\varepsilon\partial_{x}\chi_{1}\rangle
−⟨h⁡(U+ε,V+η)−h⁡(U,V),2​χ1​∂xε+ε​∂xχ1⟩\displaystyle\quad-\langle h(U+\varepsilon,V+\eta)-h(U,V),2\chi_{1}\partial_{x}\varepsilon+\varepsilon\partial_{x}\chi_{1}\rangle
−⟨ℰU,2​χ1​∂xε+ε​∂xχ1⟩.\displaystyle\quad-\langle\mathcal{E}_{U},2\chi_{1}\partial_{x}\varepsilon+\varepsilon\partial_{x}\chi_{1}\rangle.

|β1​⟨ℰU,2​χ1​∂xε+ε​∂xχ1⟩|≲t−1−θ​‖ε‖H1≲t−1−2​θ1​(log⁡t)−1.\bigg|\beta_{1}\langle\mathcal{E}_{U},2\chi_{1}\partial_{x}\varepsilon+\varepsilon\partial_{x}\chi_{1}\rangle\bigg|\lesssim t^{-1-\theta}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}\lesssim t^{-1-2\theta_{1}}(\log t)^{-1}.

|⟨h⁡(U+ε,V+η)−h⁡(U,V),ε​∂xχ1⟩|≲(log⁡t)−1​(‖ε‖H12+‖η‖H12)≲t−2​θ1​(log⁡t)−1.|\langle h(U+\varepsilon,V+\eta)-h(U,V),\varepsilon\partial_{x}\chi_{1}\rangle|\lesssim(\log t)^{-1}\left(\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\eta\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\right)\lesssim t^{-2\theta_{1}}(\log t)^{-1}.

Collecting the above estimates, we obtain

dd​t​[J1​(t,ε,η)]\displaystyle\dfrac{d}{dt}[J_{1}(t,\varepsilon,\eta)] =−2​β1​⟨χ1​∂xε,h⁡(U+ε,V+η)−h⁡(U,V)⟩\displaystyle=-2\beta_{1}\langle\chi_{1}\partial_{x}\varepsilon,h(U+\varepsilon,V+\eta)-h(U,V)\rangle
−2​β1​⟨χ1​∂xη,h⁡(V+η,U+ε)−h⁡(V,U)⟩+O⁡(t−1−2​θ1​(log⁡t)−1).\displaystyle\quad-2\beta_{1}\langle\chi_{1}\partial_{x}\eta,h(V+\eta,U+\varepsilon)-h(V,U)\rangle+O(t^{-1-2\theta_{1}}(\log t)^{-1}).

We complete the proof of (3.19) by showing the following

(3.20) ⟨∂xU,K1⟩\displaystyle\langle\partial_{x}U,K_{1}\rangle +⟨χ1​∂xε,h⁡(U+ε,V+η)−h⁡(U,V)⟩\displaystyle+\langle\chi_{1}\partial_{x}\varepsilon,h(U+\varepsilon,V+\eta)-h(U,V)\rangle
+⟨χ1​∂xη,h⁡(V+η,U+ε)−h⁡(V,U)⟩=O⁡(t−2​θ1​(log⁡t)−1).\displaystyle+\langle\chi_{1}\partial_{x}\eta,h(V+\eta,U+\varepsilon)-h(V,U)\rangle=O(t^{-2\theta_{1}}(\log t)^{-1}).

First, we prove the identity

(3.21) ⟨∂xU,K1⟩+⟨∂xε,h⁡(U+ε,V+η)−h⁡(U,V)⟩\displaystyle\langle\partial_{x}U,K_{1}\rangle+\langle\partial_{x}\varepsilon,h(U+\varepsilon,V+\eta)-h(U,V)\rangle
+⟨∂xV,K2⟩+⟨∂xη,h⁡(V+η,U+ε)−h⁡(V,U)⟩=0.\displaystyle+\langle\partial_{x}V,K_{2}\rangle+\langle\partial_{x}\eta,h(V+\eta,U+\varepsilon)-h(V,U)\rangle=0.

Indeed, we have

⟨∂xu,h⁡(u,v)⟩+⟨∂xv,h⁡(v,u)⟩=∫∂x[H⁡(u,v)]=0.\langle\partial_{x}u,h(u,v)\rangle+\langle\partial_{x}v,h(v,u)\rangle=\int\partial_{x}[H(u,v)]=0.

Applying this to u=U+θ​εu=U+\theta\varepsilon and v=V+θ​ηv=V+\theta\eta, we have that for all θ∈ℝ\theta\in\mathbb{R}

Taking the derivative with respect to θ\theta at θ=0\theta=0, we obtain

+⟨∂xV,d1​h​(V,U)​(η)⟩+⟨∂xV,d2​h​(V,U)​(ε)⟩=0.\displaystyle+\langle\partial_{x}V,d_{1}h(V,U)(\eta)\rangle+\langle\partial_{x}V,d_{2}h(V,U)(\varepsilon)\rangle=0.

We apply identity (3.21) to χ114​U\chi_{1}^{\frac{1}{4}}U, χ114​V\chi_{1}^{\frac{1}{4}}V, χ114​ε\chi_{1}^{\frac{1}{4}}\varepsilon and χ114​η\chi_{1}^{\frac{1}{4}}\eta. |⟨∂x(χ114​U),K1​χ134⟩−⟨∂xU,K1⟩|+|⟨∂x(χ114​V),K2​χ134⟩|=O⁡(t−2​θ1​(log⁡t)−1),|\langle\partial_{x}(\chi_{1}^{\frac{1}{4}}U),K_{1}\chi_{1}^{\frac{3}{4}}\rangle-\langle\partial_{x}U,K_{1}\rangle|+|\langle\partial_{x}(\chi_{1}^{\frac{1}{4}}V),K_{2}\chi_{1}^{\frac{3}{4}}\rangle|=O(t^{-2\theta_{1}}(\log t)^{-1}),

and

where σ∞\sigma_{\infty} is to be chosen satisfying

|eσ∞Ω​σ∞12​T∞−1|≤(log⁡T∞)−12.\bigg|\frac{e^{\sigma_{\infty}}}{\Omega\sigma_{\infty}^{\frac{1}{2}}T_{\infty}}-1\bigg|\leq(\log T_{\infty})^{-\frac{1}{2}}.

We refer to [20, 22] for similar bootstrap estimates.

The rest of the proof is similar to the one of Theorem 2 and we omit it.

5. Discussion

For (coupled NLS), with any coupling coefficient 0<ω<10<\omega<1, we have proved the existence of symmetric 22-solitary waves (Theorem 1) and of non-symmetric 22-solitary waves (Theorem 2) with logarithmic distance. Symmetric 22-solitons with logarithmic distance were already known in the literature for the integrable cases (ω=0\omega=0 and ω=1\omega=1) and in the scalar case (NLS). In contrast, the existence of non-symmetric 22-solitary waves with logarithmic distance is new. In particular, it does not hold for the integrable case where instead a periodic regime exists.

An interesting remaining open question is whether non-symmetric logarithmic 22-solitary waves exist for the non-integrable scalar (NLS). We conjecture that it is indeed the case, as long as p≠3p\neq 3. Indeed, the first step of the strategy used in this paper, i.e. the computation of an approximate solution involving the main interaction terms, works equally well for (NLS) as for (coupled NLS). We expect a logarithmic regime with oscillations. However, whereas (coupled NLS) enjoys two L2L^{2} conservation laws, the scalar equation (NLS) enjoys only one, which does not seem sufficient for the energy method to apply in a context of two solitons with logarithmic distance without symmetry.

A more technical original aspect of this article is the introduction of a refinement of the energy method. In previous articles using approximate solutions in the context of error terms of order t−kt^{-k} (e.g. in [20, 22, 23]), the energy method induces a loss of decay. Here, the additional correction term 𝐒\mathbf{S} in Section 3.3 allows an estimate of the remainder (εη)\big(\begin{smallmatrix}\varepsilon\\ \eta\end{smallmatrix}\big) directly related to the size of the error term (ℰUℰV)\big(\begin{smallmatrix}\mathcal{E}_{U}\\ \mathcal{E}_{V}\end{smallmatrix}\big). We believe that this general observation will be useful elsewhere.
